He cannot be discharged; he was convicted of an offense involving moral turpitude
He may be discharged if he consents
He may be discharged if Ivan and Ken agree
qs.ex: All five requisites of Rule 119, Sec. 17 must be met, including no prior conviction for an offense involving moral turpitude. Estafa is one.

qs.tw: Ken is discharged instead. On the stand, he refuses to testify according to his sworn statement.
o: No, his discharge was an acquittal
Yes. Discharge is not an acquittal if he refuses to testify according to his sworn statement
Only for perjury
No, jeopardy attached
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 18.

qs.tw: The prosecution rests. Ivan files a demurrer without leave of court. It is denied.
o: Ivan presents his evidence
Ivan loses the right to present evidence; the case is decided on the prosecution's evidence
Ivan may appeal the denial
The case is dismissed
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 23: without leave + denied = waiver of the right to present evidence.

qs.tw: Instead, Ivan first asked for leave within 5 days, got it, filed the demurrer, and it was denied.
o: He cannot present evidence
He may present his evidence
He may file certiorari against the denial right away
He must plead guilty
qs.ex: With leave + denied = he may present evidence. The denial cannot be reviewed by appeal or certiorari before judgment.

qs.tw: The demurrer is granted. The prosecution files a Rule 65 petition, saying the judge weighed the evidence wrongly.
o: Yes, certiorari corrects any error
No. A granted demurrer is an acquittal; weighing evidence wrongly is an error of judgment, not grave abuse
Yes, if filed within 60 days
Only if the offended party files it
qs.ex: A granted demurrer is an acquittal on the merits. Certiorari lies only for grave abuse amounting to lack of jurisdiction.

S.title: Judgment, new trial, and appeal
S.base: Lito is convicted of estafa by the RTC. Notice of promulgation was properly served on him.

qs.q: Lito does not attend promulgation and has no justifiable reason. What happens?
o: Promulgation is reset until he appears
The judgment is recorded and served; he loses his remedies and a warrant issues, unless within 15 days he surrenders and shows justifiable cause
The judgment is void
He is acquitted
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6: promulgation in absentia.

qs.tw: Lito attends. On day 10 he files a motion for reconsideration. He receives the denial today.
qs.q: How long does he have to appeal?
o: 5 days — the balance of 15
A fresh 15 days from receipt of the denial
30 days
None; the MR used the period
qs.ex: Fresh period rule (Neypes) applies in criminal cases (Yu v. Samson-Tatad).

qs.tw: Instead, the prosecution moves for a new trial to present evidence that would increase the penalty.
o: Yes, either party may ask
No. New trial is on the accused's motion, or by the court only with his consent
Yes, before finality
Only if the offended party joins
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 1. Reopening a conviction to raise the penalty would violate double jeopardy.

qs.tw: Lito appeals; his co-accused Mon does not. The CA acquits Lito, finding there was no deceit, so no estafa at all.
o: No, Mon did not appeal
Yes, because it is favorable and applicable to him
Only if Mon files his own appeal
Only on the civil aspect
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 11(a).

qs.tw: Instead, the CA affirms the conviction but increases the penalty.
o: No, double jeopardy
Yes. An appeal opens the whole case, and the CA may increase or reduce the penalty
Only if the prosecution also appealed
Only the SC may increase penalties
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 11. By appealing, the accused waives double jeopardy protection.

qs.tw: While the appeal is pending, Lito jumps bail.
o: Nothing; the appeal continues
Dismiss the appeal, on motion or on its own
Increase the penalty automatically
Order a new trial
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 8.

qs.tw: Rewind: right after promulgation, Lito applied for probation. Within 15 days he changes his mind and files a notice of appeal.
o: Yes, still within 15 days
No. The judgment became final when he applied for probation
Yes, if probation is denied
Only with leave of court
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 7: a judgment becomes final when the accused applies for probation.

S.title: Provisional remedies
S.base: Nora, a company cashier, is charged with estafa for converting company funds she received in her job.

qs.q: Can the company ask for preliminary attachment of Nora's property in the criminal case?
o: No, attachment is only for civil cases
Yes, if the civil action is deemed instituted, because the claim is for money converted by an employee in the course of her job
Only if she is about to leave the country
Only after conviction
qs.ex: Rule 127, Sec. 2(b).

qs.tw: The company had earlier reserved its right to file a separate civil action.
qs.q: Can it still get attachment in the criminal case?
o: Yes, attachment is always available
No. Provisional remedies in the criminal case are only for the civil action deemed instituted with it
Yes, with a bigger bond
Only on the prosecutor's motion
qs.ex: Rule 127, Sec. 1. It should seek attachment in its separate civil case.

qs.tw: Different case: an accused in a physical injuries case, with the civil action included, starts selling all his land to avoid paying damages.
o: No, only embezzlement cases qualify
Yes. The accused is disposing of his property, or about to
Only after conviction
Only if he is a public officer
qs.ex: Rule 127, Sec. 2(c).

qs.tw: Instead, the accused lives abroad.
o: No, the court has no power over foreign residents
Yes. The accused resides outside the Philippines
Only if he owns no property here
Only with DFA approval
qs.ex: Rule 127, Sec. 2(d). Another ground: the accused is about to abscond from the Philippines (Sec. 2(a)).

S.title: What the information must say, and where to file
S.base: An information charges Paolo with estafa. It names the offended party, describes the acts, and says the crime happened "on or about March 2026" in Quezon City.

qs.q: The information gives only an approximate date. Is it defective?
o: Yes, the exact date is always required
No. An approximate date is enough unless the date is a material ingredient of the offense
Yes, unless the accused consents
No, the date is never needed
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 11: it is enough to state the approximate date, unless the precise date is a material ingredient of the offense.

qs.tw: The caption calls the crime "theft," but the facts described in the body are those of estafa.
qs.q: What crime is Paolo actually charged with?
o: Theft, because the caption controls
Estafa, because the facts alleged in the body control, not the caption or designation
Neither; the information is void
Both theft and estafa
qs.ex: Jurisprudence: the nature of the crime is determined by the facts alleged in the information, not by its caption or the designation of the offense.

qs.tw: The deceit happened in Makati, and Paolo received the money in Quezon City. The information is filed in Manila, where the victim lives.
o: Yes, the victim's residence is a proper venue
No. Venue is where the offense or any of its essential ingredients happened — Makati or Quezon City
Yes, if the accused does not object
Yes, any RTC in Metro Manila may hear it
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 15(a). In criminal cases venue is jurisdictional, so the Manila court has no jurisdiction over the offense.

qs.tw: New information: it charges Paolo with estafa and, separately, slight physical injuries in a different incident. He does not object before trial, and both are proven.
o: Convict only for the first offense
Convict him of both and impose a penalty for each, stating findings separately
Dismiss the whole case for duplicity
Order the prosecutor to file a new information first
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 3: if the accused fails to object to duplicity before trial, he may be convicted of as many offenses as are charged and proved.

qs.tw: Same two-offense information, but this time Paolo moves to quash before plea.
o: Denied; duplicity is only formal
Granted on the ground that more than one offense is charged; the prosecutor may file proper informations
Granted, and no new case may be filed
Denied unless the offended party agrees
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 3(f) and Sec. 6: a quash for duplicity does not bar refiling. Rule 110, Sec. 13 requires one offense per information unless the law gives a single penalty.

qs.tw: New case: Paolo is charged with murder. The information says "with treachery" but states no facts showing treachery. He never moved to quash or asked for a bill of particulars.
qs.q: If treachery is proven at trial, can it be appreciated?
o: No, the bare word "treachery" is never enough
Yes. By not moving to quash or asking for a bill of particulars, he waived the defect
No, the information is void
Only if he pleads guilty
qs.ex: People v. Solar (2019): an information should state the facts that make up a qualifying circumstance. An accused who does not object through a motion to quash or a bill of particulars waives the defect.

S.title: The public prosecutor and the private lawyer
S.base: Quinn is the offended party in an estafa case. She hires a private lawyer. The public prosecutor is handling the case.

qs.q: Can Quinn's private lawyer appear in the case?
o: No, only the public prosecutor may appear
Yes. The offended party may intervene by counsel, since the civil action was not waived, reserved, or filed separately
Only after conviction
Only with the accused's consent
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 16.

qs.tw: Quinn had earlier reserved her right to file a separate civil action.
qs.q: Can her private lawyer still intervene in the criminal case?
o: Yes, intervention is always allowed
No. Intervention is allowed only when the civil action was not waived, reserved, or filed separately
Yes, but only to cross-examine
Only if the public prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 16.

qs.tw: Back to no reservation. The public prosecutor is absent at a hearing. The private lawyer presents prosecution witnesses on the criminal aspect without any written authority.
o: Yes, the private lawyer represents the offended party
No. The case is under the public prosecutor's direction and control; a private prosecutor needs written authority from the head prosecutor, subject to court approval
Yes, if the judge allows it orally
Yes, for light offenses only
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 5 (as amended): the private prosecutor may prosecute only with written authority of the Chief of the Prosecution Office or the Regional State Prosecutor, approved by the court.

qs.tw: After a DOJ review finds no probable cause, the public prosecutor moves to withdraw the information. The court already has the case.
qs.q: Must the judge grant the motion?
o: Yes, the prosecutor controls the case
No. Once filed in court, the case's fate rests with the court, which must make its own assessment
Yes, if the Secretary of Justice ordered it
No, withdrawals are never allowed
qs.ex: Crespo v. Mogul: once the information is filed, any disposition of the case rests in the sound discretion of the court.

qs.tw: The court dismisses the criminal case. The public prosecutor does nothing. Quinn wants to appeal the criminal aspect herself.
o: Yes, the offended party may appeal both aspects
No. Only the OSG represents the People on the criminal aspect; she may appeal only the civil aspect
Yes, if she pays docket fees
Only with the judge's permission
qs.ex: The criminal aspect belongs to the State, represented on appeal by the Solicitor General. Rule 122, Sec. 11(b): the offended party's appeal of the civil aspect does not affect the criminal aspect.

S.title: B.P. 22 and prejudicial questions
S.base: Rafa gave Sol a P500,000 check that bounced. Sol files a B.P. 22 case against Rafa.

qs.q: Sol wants to reserve the civil action and file it separately. Can she?
o: Yes, before the prosecution presents evidence
No. In B.P. 22 cases, the civil action is deemed included and no reservation is allowed
Yes, if she pays the docket fees first
Only with the court's permission
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 1(b).

qs.q: How are filing fees handled for the civil aspect?
o: They are a first lien on the judgment
Sol pays fees based on the amount of the check when she files
No fees are required in criminal cases
Rafa pays them if convicted
qs.tw: Same B.P. 22 case.
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 1(b): the offended party pays filing fees based on the amount of the check involved.

qs.tw: Before the B.P. 22 case, Sol had already filed a civil collection case, and its trial has not started.
qs.q: What may happen to that civil case?
o: It must be dismissed
It may be consolidated with the criminal case upon application
It proceeds independently
It is automatically suspended forever
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 1(b): a separately filed civil action whose trial has not started may be consolidated with the criminal case on application.

qs.tw: Rafa files a counterclaim for damages against Sol in the B.P. 22 case.
o: Yes, since the civil action is included
No. Counterclaims, cross-claims, and third-party complaints are not allowed in the criminal case; file a separate civil action
Yes, if it arises from the same check
Only after conviction
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 1(a).

qs.tw: New case: Tomas is charged with estafa. Before the criminal case, a civil case was filed whose ruling would decide whether the criminal case can proceed. The criminal case is now in court.
qs.q: When must Tomas file his petition to suspend?
o: Any time before judgment
In the same criminal case, before the prosecution rests
Only during preliminary investigation
In the civil case
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 6.

qs.tw: Change it: Tomas filed that civil case only after the criminal case was filed.
o: Yes, if the issues are related
No. A prejudicial question needs a previously instituted civil action
Yes, if the civil case is decided first
Only if the court consolidates them
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 7(a). The Continuous Trial Guidelines also treat a petition to suspend without a properly filed civil case as a prohibited motion.

S.title: Inside the preliminary investigation
S.base: Uma files a complaint for qualified theft (penalty far above 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day) with the city prosecutor against Vic.

qs.q: Vic receives a subpoena. Instead of a counter-affidavit, he files a motion to dismiss. Is that allowed?
o: Yes, any time
No. He must file a counter-affidavit within 10 days; a motion to dismiss in its place is not allowed
Yes, if he cites lack of jurisdiction
Only with leave
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 3(c).

qs.tw: Vic ignores the subpoena and files nothing.
qs.q: What does the investigating prosecutor do?
o: Wait until he appears
Resolve the complaint based on the complainant's evidence
Dismiss for lack of a counter-affidavit
Ask the court to compel him
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 3(d).

qs.tw: The investigating prosecutor finds probable cause and files the information without the city prosecutor's prior written approval.
o: None; any prosecutor may file
Lack of the head prosecutor's prior written authority — a ground to quash, which Vic must raise before plea
The information is void and cannot be cured
The court must dismiss it on its own
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 4; Rule 117, Sec. 3(d). Jurisprudence treats the defect as waivable.

qs.tw: The information is properly filed. Within 10 days, the RTC judge reads only the prosecutor's certification and issues a warrant.
o: Yes, the certification is enough
No. The judge must personally evaluate the prosecutor's resolution and its supporting evidence
Yes, the prosecutor already found probable cause
No, the judge must hold a full hearing with witnesses
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a). The judge need not personally examine witnesses, but cannot rely on the certification alone.

qs.tw: The judge has doubts about probable cause.
o: Dismiss right away
Order the prosecutor to present additional evidence within 5 days, and resolve within 30 days from filing
Conduct his own preliminary investigation
Refer the case to the DOJ
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a).

qs.tw: Instead, the evidence clearly fails to show probable cause.
o: Issue the warrant anyway
Immediately dismiss the case
Return the records to the prosecutor
Wait for a motion
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a).

qs.tw: Rewind: the city prosecutor dismissed Uma's complaint. Uma petitions the Secretary of Justice, who reverses.
o: No, the city prosecutor's ruling is final
Yes. The Secretary of Justice may reverse or modify and direct the filing of an information
Only if the RTC approves
Only if Vic consents
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 4.

S.title: Hot pursuit, methods, and escapes
S.base: Police arrive at a market ten minutes after a stabbing. They see the victim, hear eyewitnesses describe a man in a green shirt who just ran off, and find a man in a blood-stained green shirt nearby.

qs.q: Can they arrest him without a warrant?
o: No, they did not see the stabbing
Yes. The offense was just committed, and they have probable cause based on facts they personally gathered right away
Only if he confesses
Only with a barangay official present
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 5(b): hot pursuit — offense just committed, plus probable cause based on personal knowledge of facts and circumstances.

qs.tw: Instead, police arrest him three days later, based only on a witness's statement.
o: Yes, under hot pursuit
No. The offense was not "just committed," and they lack personal knowledge; they need a warrant
Yes, because there is an eyewitness
Yes, within 7 days
qs.ex: Hot pursuit needs immediacy and personal knowledge.

qs.tw: Police get a warrant. The arresting officer does not have it with him. The suspect demands to see it.
o: No, the warrant must be in hand
Yes. The officer need not have it in his possession, but must show it as soon as practicable after the arrest if asked
Only if the suspect consents
No, the suspect may refuse
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 7.

qs.tw: The suspect runs into his house and refuses to open the door.
o: Wait for a search warrant
Break in, after announcing his authority and purpose and being refused admittance
Nothing; homes are inviolable
Only call the suspect's lawyer
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 11.

qs.tw: Different scene: a private citizen sees a man snatch a bag and grabs him.
o: No, only officers may arrest
Yes. A private person may arrest in the same situations, and must deliver him to the nearest police station or jail
Only with a barangay official
Only if the citizen is a lawyer
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 5.

qs.tw: The arrested man escapes from jail a week later.
qs.q: Do police need a warrant to recapture him?
o: Yes, a new warrant
No. An escaped person may be pursued and retaken without a warrant, at any time and anywhere in the Philippines
Only within the same city
Only within 24 hours
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 13.

S.title: Bail: how it works day to day
S.base: Wena is charged with estafa (bailable as a matter of right). She is out on a property bond.

qs.q: Until when does her bail stay in force?
o: Until arraignment
At all stages until promulgation of the RTC judgment, unless cancelled
Until the prosecution rests
Until the case reaches the Supreme Court
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 2(a).

qs.tw: Wena, already arraigned, skips a trial date without justification despite notice.
o: It must be postponed until she appears
She is deemed to waive her right to be present; trial may proceed in absentia
The case is dismissed
She is automatically convicted
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 2(c); Rule 115, Sec. 1(c). Trial in absentia needs arraignment, notice, and unjustified absence.

qs.tw: The court declares her bond forfeited.
o: Pay immediately
Within 30 days, produce her and explain why judgment should not be rendered against them
Nothing; forfeiture is final
Ask for a new bond
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 21. If they fail, judgment is rendered against them jointly and severally.

qs.tw: Wena is acquitted.
o: The bondsmen must apply to cancel it
It is automatically cancelled
It stays until appeal
It is forfeited
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 22: automatically cancelled on acquittal, dismissal, or execution of a judgment of conviction.

qs.tw: Rewind: Wena could not post bail and has been detained for as long as the maximum imprisonment for the offense.
o: She stays until judgment
She is released immediately, without prejudice to the trial continuing
She must post a reduced bail
She is acquitted
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 16.

qs.tw: Out on bail, Wena tries to fly abroad without the court's permission.
qs.q: Can she be arrested without a warrant?
o: No, she has bail
Yes. An accused on bail may be re-arrested without a warrant if she tries to leave the Philippines without permission
Only by her bondsman
Only after her bail is cancelled
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 23.

qs.tw: Before arraignment, Wena (out on bail) moves to quash the warrant for lack of probable cause.
o: Yes, bail waives all objections
No. Bail does not bar challenges to the arrest, warrant, or PI if raised before plea
Yes, unless the bail was cash
Only if the prosecutor objects
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 26.

qs.tw: New accused: Xyla, still at large and not arrested, files a petition for bail.
o: Yes, bail is a right
No. Bail requires that she be in the custody of the law
Yes, if she pays double
Only for light offenses
qs.ex: Jurisprudence (e.g., Paderanga v. CA): only a person in custody, by arrest or voluntary surrender, may apply for bail.

S.title: Pleas, plea bargaining, and pre-trial
S.base: Yuri is charged with murder. At arraignment, the victim's family (the offended party) and the prosecutor are present.

qs.q: Yuri offers to plead guilty to homicide. What is needed?
o: Only the judge's approval
Consent of the offended party and the prosecutor, and the court's approval
Only the prosecutor's consent
An amended information
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 2: plea to a lesser offense necessarily included in the charge, with consent of the offended party and prosecutor. No amendment needed.

qs.tw: The offended party does not appear at arraignment despite due notice.
qs.q: Can the plea to homicide still be accepted?
o: No, the offended party must always consent
Yes, with the conformity of the trial prosecutor alone
Only after a postponement
Only if Yuri pays damages first
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 1(f).

qs.tw: Yuri pleaded not guilty at arraignment. Before trial, he wants to plead guilty to homicide.
o: Yes, after arraignment no change is allowed
No. After arraignment but before trial, he may withdraw his not-guilty plea and plead to the lesser offense
Only with a new information
Only during trial
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 2.

qs.tw: Yuri pleaded guilty to homicide. Before the judgment becomes final, he says he did not understand the plea.
o: No, a guilty plea is final
Yes. The court may allow an improvident plea of guilty to be withdrawn any time before the judgment becomes final
Only before sentencing
Only on appeal
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 5.

qs.tw: Rewind: the information is vague about how Yuri took part. Before arraignment, he asks for a bill of particulars.
o: No, bills of particulars are for civil cases
Yes, if filed before arraignment and it specifies the defects and details wanted
Only after the prosecution rests
Only if the prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 9.

qs.tw: At arraignment, Yuri appears unable to understand the charge because of an unsound mental condition.
o: Enter a not-guilty plea
Suspend the arraignment and order a mental examination
Proceed, because counsel is present
Dismiss the case
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 11(a).

qs.tw: Yuri stays outside the courtroom, and his lawyer enters a plea of not guilty for him.
o: Yes, counsel may plead for the accused
No. The accused must be present and personally enter his plea
Yes, if the court records it
Yes, for not-guilty pleas only
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 1(b).

qs.tw: At pre-trial, Yuri's lawyer signs a written stipulation admitting Yuri was at the scene. Yuri does not sign it.
qs.q: Can the stipulation be used against Yuri?
o: Yes, counsel binds the client
No. Pre-trial admissions must be in writing and signed by both the accused and counsel
Yes, if the court approved it
Only on the civil aspect
qs.ex: Rule 118, Sec. 2.

S.title: More quash grounds and jeopardy exceptions
S.base: Zed is charged with a light offense. The information was filed after the offense had already prescribed.

o: The facts charged do not constitute an offense
The criminal action or liability has been extinguished
The court has no jurisdiction over his person
The information does not conform to the prescribed form
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 3(g). Prescription extinguishes criminal liability.

qs.tw: Zed raises prescription only on appeal, after conviction.
o: Yes, it should have been raised before plea
No. Extinction of liability is never waived
Yes, unless the prosecution agrees
Only on the civil aspect
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 9.

qs.tw: New case: an MTC tries Zed for an offense that belongs to the RTC. He is arraigned and convicted. The case is then refiled in the RTC.
qs.q: Is the RTC case barred by double jeopardy?
o: Yes, he was already convicted
No. The first court had no jurisdiction, so no jeopardy attached
Yes, because he was arraigned
No, but he gets credit for time served
qs.ex: First jeopardy needs a court of competent jurisdiction (Rule 117, Sec. 7). Lack of jurisdiction over the offense is never waived.

qs.tw: Zed was never validly arrested, but he posted bail, was arraigned, and only then moved to quash for lack of jurisdiction over his person.
o: Yes, jurisdiction over the person is never waived
No. He submitted to the court's jurisdiction and did not raise it before plea
Yes, because the arrest was invalid
Only if the prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Lack of jurisdiction over the person is waivable (it is not among a, b, g, i). Objections must be raised before plea (Rule 114, Sec. 26; Rule 117, Sec. 9).

qs.tw: Zed was convicted of slight physical injuries after pleading guilty to that lesser offense without the prosecutor's or offended party's consent. He is now charged with serious physical injuries for the same act.
o: Yes, double jeopardy
No. A plea to a lesser offense without their consent does not bar the graver charge
Yes, unless new evidence appeared
No, but only if he consents
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 7(c). He is credited for any part of the sentence served.

qs.tw: Instead, the facts making up the graver offense existed at the time of his plea but were discovered only afterward.
o: Yes, the facts already existed
No. Facts discovered only after the plea allow the graver charge
Yes, unless he consents
Only if the victim died
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 7(b).

qs.tw: Different information: its own allegations show that Zed acted in lawful self-defense.
o: The facts do not constitute an offense
It contains averments that, if true, would be a legal excuse or justification
Lack of jurisdiction
Double jeopardy
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 3(h).

S.title: Trial procedure and witnesses
S.base: Abel is on trial for homicide.

qs.q: Abel admits killing the victim but claims self-defense. Can the order of trial change?
o: No, the prosecution always goes first
Yes. When the accused admits the act but claims a lawful defense, the order may be modified (reverse trial)
Only if the prosecution agrees
Only in civil cases
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 11(e).

qs.tw: A key prosecution witness is about to leave the Philippines with no definite date of return.
qs.q: How can the testimony be preserved?
o: It cannot; wait for the witness
Conditional examination before the court where the case is pending, with Abel present or notified
By affidavit only
By deposition before a notary abroad
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 15.

qs.tw: Instead, a defense witness is sick and lives more than 100 km away with no means to travel.
qs.q: Before whom may the witness be conditionally examined?
o: Only the trial court
A judge, a member of the bar in good standing designated by the judge, or an inferior court judge
Any notary public
The prosecutor
qs.ex: Rule 119, Secs. 12–13.

qs.tw: A witness testified in an earlier case with the same parties and subject matter, where Abel cross-examined him. The witness has since died.
qs.q: Can that earlier testimony be used against Abel?
o: No, it violates confrontation
Yes. Prior testimony of an unavailable witness may be used where the adverse party had a chance to cross-examine
Only if Abel agrees
Only in the civil aspect
qs.ex: Rule 115, Sec. 1(f).

qs.tw: Before he was ever arraigned, a co-accused, Bart, escaped.
qs.q: Can Bart be tried in absentia?
o: Yes, trial in absentia is allowed for fugitives
No. Trial in absentia requires that the accused was first arraigned
Yes, if counsel is appointed
Yes, after 30 days
qs.ex: Constitution and Rule 115, Sec. 1(c): requisites are arraignment, due notice, and unjustified absence.

qs.tw: Trial has gone on for over 180 days because of prosecution delays. Abel never moved to dismiss before trial. Now, after trial, he moves to dismiss for violation of speedy trial.
qs.q: Will the motion prosper under Rule 119?
o: Yes, the 180-day limit was violated
No. Failure to move for dismissal before trial waives the right to dismissal under Rule 119, Sec. 9
Yes, automatically
Only with the prosecutor's consent
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 9. The constitutional right to speedy trial remains a separate basis (Sec. 10).

qs.tw: Different case: Cora is charged with estafa, but the evidence shows only theft, which is not included in estafa. Judgment has not yet been rendered.
o: Acquit her right away
Not discharge her if there is good cause to detain; commit her for the proper offense and dismiss the original case once the proper information is filed
Convict her of theft
Convict her of estafa
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 19.

qs.tw: Back to Abel. After both sides rest but before judgment, a new witness surfaces.
qs.q: Can the judge reopen the proceedings?
o: No, the case is submitted
Yes. Before finality of a judgment of conviction, the judge may reopen, motu proprio or on motion, with a hearing, to avoid miscarriage of justice
Only on the prosecution's motion
Only on appeal
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 24. The reopened proceedings must end within 30 days.

S.title: Judgment contents, promulgation, and new trial
S.base: Bea is tried for theft in an RTC in Cebu.

qs.q: The judge acquits Bea, writing only: "The accused is not guilty." Is the judgment complete?
o: Yes, an acquittal needs no explanation
No. It must state whether the evidence absolutely failed or merely failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and whether the act giving rise to civil liability existed
Yes, if the prosecutor does not object
No, it must also fix the penalty
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 2.

qs.tw: Rewind: Bea is convicted. She is detained in a Davao jail.
o: The Cebu judge must travel to Davao
The executive judge of the RTC with jurisdiction over the place of confinement, upon the Cebu court's request
Any Davao clerk of court
It must wait until she is brought to Cebu
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6.

qs.tw: Bea is in Cebu, but the judge is absent on the promulgation date.
o: Nobody; reset it
The clerk of court
The prosecutor
Bea's counsel
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6: the clerk may promulgate when the judge is absent or outside the province or city.

qs.tw: Different case: Bea is convicted of a light offense. She is absent, but her counsel is present.
o: No, she must be present
Yes. For a light offense, judgment may be pronounced in the presence of counsel or a representative
Only after a warrant is served
Only if she consents in writing
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6.

qs.tw: Back to the theft conviction. Bea moves for new trial, offering a witness she knew about before trial but did not call.
o: Yes, any new witness is enough
No. Evidence that could have been found and presented with reasonable diligence is not newly discovered
Yes, if the witness is credible
Only if the prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 2(b).

qs.tw: Instead, new trial is granted on truly newly discovered evidence.
qs.q: What happens to the evidence already presented?
o: It is all set aside
It stands; the new evidence is added
Only the defense evidence stands
Only documents stand
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 6(b).

qs.tw: Instead, new trial is granted because of an irregularity that prejudiced Bea at trial.
o: All evidence stands
The proceedings and evidence affected are set aside and taken anew
The case is dismissed
The judgment is affirmed
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 6(a).

qs.tw: The judgment has become final. Bea now moves for new trial in the RTC.
o: Yes, any time
No. New trial must be sought before the judgment of conviction becomes final
Yes, on newly discovered evidence
Only with the prosecutor's consent
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 1.

S.title: Appeal routes and higher courts
S.base: Cris is convicted in a criminal case.

qs.q: Cris was convicted by an MTC, which followed the same procedure as an RTC. Where and how does he appeal?
o: To the CA by petition for review
To the RTC by notice of appeal
To the SC by certiorari
To the RTC by petition for review
qs.ex: Rule 122, Secs. 2(a), 3(a). Rule 123: MTCs follow the same procedure as RTCs, except RTC-only provisions and summary procedure.

qs.tw: The RTC affirms on appeal. Cris wants to go to the CA.
o: Notice of appeal
Petition for review under Rule 42
Petition for certiorari under Rule 65
Automatic review
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 3(b): from the RTC in its appellate jurisdiction.

qs.tw: Different case: Cris was tried by the RTC and sentenced to reclusion perpetua.
o: Petition for review on certiorari to the SC
Notice of appeal to the CA
Automatic review by the SC
Petition for review to the CA
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 3(c).

qs.tw: The CA affirms reclusion perpetua.
qs.q: How does he go to the SC?
o: Petition for review on certiorari
Notice of appeal filed with the CA
Automatic review
Motion for reconsideration only
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 13(c).

qs.tw: Instead, the CA affirms a 10-year sentence.
qs.q: How does he go to the SC?
o: Notice of appeal
Petition for review on certiorari (Rule 45)
Automatic review
Petition for review (Rule 42)
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 3(e); Rule 125, Sec. 2.

qs.tw: At the CA, Cris's counsel de oficio fails to file the appellant's brief on time.
qs.q: Can the CA dismiss the appeal for this?
o: Yes, failure to file a brief is always fatal
No. The CA may not dismiss for failure to file a brief when the appellant is represented by counsel de oficio
Yes, after 30 days
Only if the OSG asks
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 8.

qs.tw: Back at the trial court, Cris filed a notice of appeal but now wants to withdraw it. The records have not yet been forwarded.
o: No, an appeal cannot be withdrawn
Yes. The trial court may allow it, and the judgment becomes final
Only with the CA's approval
Only if the prosecution agrees
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 12.

qs.tw: The offended party appeals only the amount of civil damages.
qs.q: Does this affect Cris's criminal conviction?
o: Yes, the whole case reopens
No. An appeal of the civil aspect does not affect the criminal aspect
Yes, the penalty may be increased
Only if Cris also appeals
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 11(b).

qs.tw: While the appeal is pending at the CA, Cris discovers new evidence material to his defense.
o: Nothing; wait for the CA decision
Move for new trial at the CA before its judgment becomes final
File a new case
Go straight to the SC
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 14.

qs.tw: The case reaches the SC en banc. The Justices are equally divided on acquittal, and re-deliberation does not break the tie.
o: The conviction is affirmed
The conviction is reversed and Cris is acquitted
The case is remanded
The Chief Justice decides
qs.ex: Rule 125, Sec. 3.

S.title: Getting and serving a search warrant
S.base: Police want a search warrant for Dina's house in Pasig for illegal firearms. No criminal case has been filed.

o: Any court in the Philippines
Any court within whose territorial jurisdiction the crime was committed; or, for compelling reasons stated, any court in the judicial region
Only the Supreme Court
Only the court of the police station's location
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 2.

qs.tw: A criminal case for the same offense is already pending in a Pasig RTC branch.
o: Any Pasig court
Only the court where the criminal case is pending
Any court in the region
The executive judge
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 2 (last paragraph).

qs.tw: The judge issues the warrant after reading only the applicant's affidavit, without asking any questions.
o: Yes, the affidavit is under oath
No. The judge must personally examine the applicant and witnesses through searching questions and answers, in writing and under oath
Yes, if the affidavit is detailed
Only if the prosecutor signed
qs.ex: Rule 126, Secs. 4–5.

qs.tw: The warrant says nothing about the time of service. Police search at 11 p.m.
o: Yes, any time is fine
No. A warrant must be served in the daytime unless the affidavit says the property is on the person or in the place, and the warrant allows service at any time
Yes, if the occupant is awake
Only on weekends
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 9.

qs.tw: Police seize the guns. Dina is present, but they leave no receipt.
qs.q: What did they fail to do?
o: Nothing
Give the lawful occupant a detailed receipt for the property seized
Call the media
Photograph the house
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 11.

qs.tw: Police bring the seized items to their headquarters and keep them there.
o: Yes, police hold evidence
No. They must deliver the property to the issuing judge, with a true inventory verified under oath
Yes, for 30 days
Only if no case is filed
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 12(a).

qs.tw: While validly searching for guns, officers see a bag of shabu lying openly on a table.
o: No, the warrant covers only firearms
Yes, under plain view: they were lawfully there, came upon it inadvertently, and its illegal character was immediately apparent
Only with a second warrant
Only if Dina consents
qs.ex: Plain view doctrine.

qs.tw: Instead, they pry open a locked drawer, find personal letters unrelated to firearms, and seize them.
o: Yes, they were found during a valid search
No. They are outside the warrant and not in plain view
Yes, if they are relevant
Only on the civil aspect
qs.ex: The warrant limits what may be seized; plain view requires the item to be visible without further search.

qs.tw: Dina wants to quash the warrant. No criminal case has been filed yet.
qs.q: Where does she file the motion?
o: Any court
The court that issued the warrant
The DOJ
The Court of Appeals
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 14. Once a criminal case is filed, the motion goes to the court where it is filed.

S.title: The 2017 Continuous Trial Guidelines
S.base: Rico is charged with estafa in the RTC. The case is governed by the Revised Guidelines for Continuous Trial of Criminal Cases (A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC).

qs.q: Before arraignment, Rico moves to quash because the complainant has since signed an affidavit of desistance. How should the court treat the motion?
o: Deny it outright as a prohibited motion
Set it for hearing; every motion to quash deserves one
Grant it; the offended party no longer wants to prosecute
Hold it until the prosecution comments
qs.ex: A motion to quash not based on a ground in Rule 117, Sec. 3 is a prohibited motion under the Guidelines and is denied outright, without need of comment. An affidavit of desistance is not a ground to quash, nor to dismiss once the case is in court (People v. Ramirez).

qs.tw: Rico was in fact arrested without a warrant, and the information was filed after inquest. Eight days after learning of the filing, he moves for a preliminary investigation.
o: It is granted; PI is part of due process
It is denied outright as prohibited; it was filed after the 5-day period
It suspends the trial for 60 days
It is granted if he waives Art. 125 of the RPC
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 6 gives the accused 5 days from learning of the filing to ask for a PI. Under the Guidelines, a motion for PI filed after the 5 days is a prohibited motion.

qs.tw: At trial, the prosecutor moves to postpone because his witness has a hearing in another court that day.
o: Yes, a conflicting schedule is good cause
No. Postponement is allowed only for acts of God, force majeure, or physical inability of the witness to appear
Yes, if the defense agrees
Yes, once for each party
qs.ex: The Guidelines prohibit motions for postponement except for acts of God, force majeure, or the physical inability of the witness to appear and testify.

qs.tw: Instead, the witness is hospitalized on the hearing date, and the court grants the postponement.
qs.q: What else applies to the prosecution?
o: Nothing; the trial calendar is simply reset
It must pay the postponement fee and still finish its evidence on the dates already agreed
It must ask the Supreme Court to extend the 180-day trial period
It must take the witness's deposition abroad
qs.ex: A motion for postponement, written or oral, must come with the official receipt of the postponement fee (Rule 141, Sec. 21[b]). The movant is warned that its evidence must still be completed on the dates previously agreed.

qs.tw: The witness recovers. Her direct examination runs past noon.
qs.q: May her cross-examination be moved to another hearing date?
o: Yes, cross-examination may take several hearings
As a rule no; a witness must be fully examined in one day
Only if she is an expert witness
Yes, on a written motion of the defense
qs.ex: The Guidelines adopt the one-day examination of witness rule: each witness is fully examined in one day.

qs.tw: The prosecution presents its last witness.
qs.q: How does it offer its documentary exhibits?
o: By a written formal offer within 15 days
Orally, that same day; the defense objects at once and the court rules in open court
In its memorandum
No offer is needed for exhibits marked at pre-trial
qs.ex: Under the Guidelines, the offer of evidence, the objection, and the ruling are made orally, on the day the last witness is presented. Exhibits marked but never offered are not evidence (Rule 132, Sec. 34).

qs.tw: On the defense's first trial date, Rico's counsel de parte does not show up.
o: Postpone; Rico has a right to counsel of his choice
Proceed, after appointing a counsel de oficio for the hearing
Declare that Rico waived his evidence
Cite counsel in contempt and reset
qs.ex: Under the Guidelines, if counsel de parte is absent, the hearing proceeds upon the appointment of a counsel de oficio.

S.title: Demurrer under the Guidelines
S.base: Lea is charged with malversation in the RTC. The prosecution has just rested its case.

qs.q: Under the Guidelines, what does the court do first?
o: Dismiss the case on its own if the evidence looks weak
Ask Lea whether she will move for leave to file a demurrer or present her evidence
Require memoranda from both sides
Submit the case for decision
qs.ex: The Guidelines direct the court to ask the accused whether she wants to move for leave to file a demurrer or to proceed with her evidence. The court may still dismiss on its own under Rule 119, Sec. 23, but only after hearing the prosecution.

qs.tw: Lea's counsel moves for leave orally, right there in court.
qs.q: Is an oral motion for leave allowed?
o: No, it must be written, state its grounds, and be filed within 5 days
Yes; the Guidelines allow an oral motion for leave, resolved orally
Only with the prosecutor's consent
Only in first-level courts
qs.ex: The Guidelines expressly allow an oral motion for leave, which the court resolves orally. The written 5-day motion is the Rules of Court route.

qs.tw: Leave is denied. Lea files her demurrer anyway.
o: The demurrer is stricken and she must present evidence
It is treated as filed without leave: her evidence dates are cancelled, and if it is denied she can no longer present evidence
She may question the denial of leave by certiorari right away
The case is dismissed for her defiance
qs.ex: Under the Guidelines, if the accused insists on filing the demurrer after leave is denied, the scheduled dates for her evidence are cancelled. If the demurrer is then denied, she waives the right to present evidence (Rule 119, Sec. 23).

qs.tw: Instead, leave is granted. Lea files her demurrer within 10 days, and the prosecution comments within 10 days after.
qs.q: Within what period must the court resolve the demurrer?
o: 10 days
30 days from the comment (or the lapse of the period to comment)
90 days
3 months, the constitutional period
qs.ex: Under the Guidelines: demurrer within 10 days from the grant of leave; comment within 10 days; resolution within a non-extendible 30 days.

qs.tw: Different timing: before the prosecution has made its formal offer, Lea moves to dismiss because the case has dragged on for years. The court treats it as a demurrer without leave, denies it, and rules that she waived her evidence.
o: Yes, any motion to dismiss on the evidence is a demurrer
No. A motion based on speedy trial, filed before the prosecution rested, is not a demurrer; she keeps her right to present evidence
Yes, because she did not ask for leave
No, because demurrers are not allowed in malversation
qs.ex: Cabador v. People (2009): look at good faith, the stage of filing, and the main objective. A demurrer assumes the prosecution has rested and attacks the sufficiency of its evidence. A demurrer filed before the prosecution rests is premature.

qs.tw: Back to a proper demurrer, filed with leave. It is granted, and in the same order the court clears Lea of all civil liability without hearing her evidence on it.
o: Yes, an acquittal always carries civil absolution
No. Unless the act giving rise to civil liability did not exist, the court must hear the accused on the civil aspect
Yes, malversation has no civil aspect
No, the civil aspect must always be filed separately
qs.ex: Salazar v. People (2003): granting a demurrer does not let the court decide the civil aspect at once, since the accused has not presented evidence on it; trial continues on the civil aspect unless the act did not exist.

qs.tw: Rewind: Lea filed her demurrer without leave, and it was denied.
qs.q: What does the court decide next?
o: Only the criminal aspect
The whole case, civil aspect included, on the prosecution's evidence (unless the civil action was reserved or waived)
Nothing until the prosecution presents rebuttal
Whether to let her present evidence after all
qs.ex: Hun Hyung Park v. Eung Won Choi (2007): a denied demurrer without leave submits the whole case, including its civil aspect, for judgment on the prosecution's evidence.

S.title: Remedies after a conviction
S.base: Carlo is convicted of homicide by the RTC. The judgment is promulgated on March 1, in his presence.

qs.q: On March 10, a store owner tells Carlo's lawyer that her CCTV, which she never checked because she was abroad during the trial, shows someone else stabbing the victim. What should Carlo file, and by when?
o: A motion for reconsideration by March 31
A motion for new trial on newly discovered evidence by March 16, with the owner's affidavit and an authenticated copy of the video
A petition for certiorari within 60 days
A motion to reopen, any time before he serves his sentence
qs.ex: Rule 121, Secs. 1, 2(b), 4: new trial on newly discovered evidence, filed within the 15-day period, supported by affidavits or duly authenticated documents, with notice to the prosecutor.

qs.tw: No motion is filed. On March 5, the judge, troubled by the case, orders a new trial on his own, over Carlo's objection.
o: Yes, the court may always order a new trial on its own
No. The court may grant a new trial on its own initiative only with the accused's consent
Yes, to avoid a miscarriage of justice
No, only the prosecution may ask for it
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 1: the court may grant a new trial or reconsideration on motion of the accused, or at its own instance but with the consent of the accused.

qs.tw: Instead, on March 5 Carlo files a written waiver of his right to appeal.
qs.q: When does the judgment become final?
o: March 16, when the appeal period ends
March 5, upon the written waiver
Only upon entry of judgment
Only when he starts serving his sentence
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 7: a judgment of conviction becomes final when the period to appeal lapses, when the sentence is partly or fully served, when the accused waives appeal in writing, or when he applies for probation.

qs.tw: No waiver. On March 8, Carlo asks the judge to lower his penalty because a mitigating circumstance was overlooked.
qs.q: Which remedy fits, and can the judge do it without being asked?
o: Modification of judgment; only on the accused's motion, before finality or perfection of appeal
Reopening; the judge may do it on his own, without a hearing
Modification; the judge may do it on his own
Only an appeal will do
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 7: modification is only on the accused's motion and needs no hearing. Reopening (Rule 119, Sec. 24) may be done motu proprio but always with a hearing, and must end in 30 days.

qs.tw: Different path: Carlo, out on bail, skipped promulgation without reason. He later files a motion for reconsideration, and the judge grants it and acquits him.
o: Yes, an acquittal is final and unappealable
No. Having lost his remedies, his MR should have been dismissed outright; the acquittal is void and jeopardy does not attach
Yes, because he eventually appeared
No, because only an appeal can reverse a conviction
qs.ex: Javier v. Gonzales (2017): entertaining the MR of an accused who lost his remedies under Rule 120, Sec. 6 is a blatant abuse of authority; the resulting acquittal is void and does not trigger double jeopardy. Jaylo v. Sandiganbayan (2015): he lost his standing in court.

qs.tw: Same absence, but Carlo surrenders on day 10 after promulgation, moves for leave, and proves he was hospitalized.
o: Nothing; his remedies were lost the moment he missed promulgation
File an MR, MNT, or appeal within 15 days from notice of the order granting leave
Appeal within the balance of the original 15 days only
Ask for a new promulgation
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6: within 15 days from promulgation, the absent accused may surrender and move for leave. If his absence was justified, he may avail of the remedies within 15 days from notice.

S.title: Appeal: who benefits and what is reviewed
S.base: Ramon and Sonny, as co-conspirators, are convicted of murder by the RTC.

qs.q: Only Ramon appeals. Sonny's 15 days lapse. Is the execution of the judgment against Sonny stayed by Ramon's appeal?
o: Yes, an appeal stays execution for all the accused
No. The stay applies only to the appealing party; the period kept running against Sonny
Yes, until the appellate court decides
Only if Sonny posts bail
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 11(c); Lubrica v. People (2007): the stay of execution cannot be extended to an accused who did not appeal.

qs.tw: Both appealed, but Sonny later withdrew his appeal and his conviction became final. The SC then downgrades Ramon's crime to homicide because the qualifying circumstance was not proved.
o: No, he withdrew his appeal
Yes. A favorable judgment applicable to him benefits him, whether or not he appealed or withdrew
No, his judgment is already final
Only if the prosecution agrees
qs.ex: People v. Valdez (2013): Sec. 11(a) applies regardless of whether a co-accused appealed or withdrew, as long as the judgment is favorable and applicable to him. Acting in conspiracy, they deserve equal liability.

qs.tw: Suppose instead the SC acquitted Ramon only because of his personal alibi.
o: Yes, any acquittal of a co-accused benefits all
No; the ruling is favorable to Ramon but not applicable to Sonny
Yes, because they were charged in one information
Only if Sonny is still detained
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 11(a): the judgment must be favorable and applicable to the non-appealing accused. Ramon's alibi says nothing about Sonny's participation.

qs.tw: Different path: the CA affirms Ramon's conviction with reclusion perpetua. Ramon files a Rule 45 petition arguing that the eyewitness was not credible.
qs.q: Will the SC review the credibility issue?
o: Yes, an appeal opens the whole case
No. Rule 45 raises only questions of law; to reopen the facts he should have filed a notice of appeal
Yes, because the penalty is reclusion perpetua
No, the SC never reviews RP cases
qs.ex: Dungo v. People (2015): when the CA imposes RP or life, the accused may file a notice of appeal (the whole case open) or a Rule 45 petition, which raises only questions of law. Credibility is a question of fact.

qs.tw: Different path: the RTC acquits Ramon. The victim's heirs want to appeal the award of damages.
qs.q: May they, and in what period?
o: No, an acquittal ends everything
Yes, within the same 15 days given to the accused; their appeal does not affect the acquittal
Yes, but only through the OSG
Yes, within 30 days
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 11(b); Ching v. Nicdao (2007): the offended party may appeal the civil aspect within the same period as the accused. The appeal does not affect the criminal aspect.

qs.tw: Different case: Ramon was convicted by the MTC and appealed to the RTC. He never filed the memorandum the RTC allowed.
qs.q: May the RTC dismiss his appeal for that?
o: Yes, just as in civil appeals under Rule 40
No. In criminal appeals to the RTC, memoranda are optional, so not filing one is no ground to dismiss
Yes, on the prosecution's motion
Only if he is out on bail
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 9(c); Sanico v. People (2015). The RTC decides on the entire record and whatever memoranda were filed.

qs.tw: In that RTC appeal, Ramon asks the RTC to hear a new witness.
qs.q: May the RTC receive the new evidence?
o: Yes, an appeal to the RTC is a trial de novo
No. The RTC decides on the record and memoranda; it does not receive new evidence or hold a trial
Yes, if the witness is newly discovered
Yes, but only documents
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 9(c): the RTC decides on the entire record and the memoranda. Unlike the CA (Rule 124, Sec. 12), it does not take evidence on appeal.

qs.tw: Different case in the CA: the record shows an error at trial that did not affect Ramon's substantial rights.
o: Yes, any error requires reversal
No. Harmless error: reverse only for errors that injuriously affect the appellant's substantial rights
Yes, if the error was assigned
Only if the prosecution admits it
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 10: no judgment shall be reversed or modified unless the error injuriously affects the substantial rights of the appellant.

S.title: Quasi-offenses, revivals, and void acquittals
S.base: Ivan, driving recklessly, hits Tess's car. Tess suffers slight injuries, her husband dies, and the car is wrecked.

qs.q: Two informations are filed: reckless imprudence resulting in slight physical injuries, and reckless imprudence resulting in homicide and damage to property. Ivan pleads guilty to the first and is sentenced. May he quash the second?
o: No; slight physical injuries cannot be complexed with homicide, so they are different offenses
Yes. Reckless imprudence is a single quasi-offense; his conviction bars the second case
No; double jeopardy does not apply to quasi-offenses
Yes, but only as to the damage to property
qs.ex: Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro (2010): the law punishes the negligent act, not its results. One reckless act is one quasi-offense, which cannot be split into separate prosecutions.

qs.tw: Different facts: Ivan punched Tess and was convicted of slight physical injuries. Weeks later, Tess dies from the same blow.
qs.q: May Ivan now be charged with homicide?
o: No, that is double jeopardy
Yes. The graver offense developed from a supervening fact arising from the same act
Only if he consents
Only if the first conviction was on a plea of guilty
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 7(a): a conviction does not bar a graver offense that developed from supervening facts arising from the same act. He gets credit for the time served.

qs.tw: Different case: Ivan's homicide case drags on. On Ivan's motion, with notice to the heirs, the court provisionally dismisses it. Homicide is punishable by reclusion temporal.
qs.q: The prosecution revives it 18 months later. Too late?
o: Yes, the one-year period has passed
No. For offenses punishable by more than 6 years, the dismissal becomes permanent only after 2 years
Yes, revival must be within 6 months
No, there is never a time limit
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 8: one year for offenses punishable by not more than 6 years or a fine; two years for those punishable by more than 6 years.

qs.tw: Instead, the dismissal was ordered on the prosecutor's motion, with no express consent from Ivan and no notice to the heirs.
qs.q: Does the 2-year time-bar of Sec. 8 apply?
o: Yes, after 2 years it becomes permanent
No. The time-bar operates only for a provisional dismissal with the accused's express consent and notice to the offended party
Yes, but it is 1 year
No, and nothing at all bars a refiling
qs.ex: Riano, citing People v. Lacson: without the requisites of the first paragraph of Sec. 8, the time-bar does not operate. Prescription or double jeopardy may still apply. A dismissal after arraignment without the accused's express consent may itself bar a new case.

qs.tw: Instead, before arraignment, the prosecutor withdraws the information to reinvestigate, and the court grants it. Three years later, a new information is filed.
qs.q: Is the new information barred by the Sec. 8 time-bar?
o: Yes, more than 2 years have passed
No. A withdrawal is not a provisional dismissal; it is without prejudice to refiling after reinvestigation
Yes, a withdrawal is an acquittal
No, but only because Ivan consented
qs.ex: Riano: a motion to withdraw the information differs from a motion to dismiss. A withdrawal is without prejudice to refiling upon reinvestigation and is not within Sec. 8. Prescription still applies.

qs.tw: Instead, the case goes to trial, and the judge acquits Ivan after refusing to let the prosecution present any witnesses.
qs.q: Can the acquittal be set aside?
o: No, an acquittal is always final
Yes, by certiorari: denying the prosecution due process is grave abuse; the acquittal is void and jeopardy does not attach
Yes, by ordinary appeal
Yes, by a motion for new trial by the prosecution
qs.ex: Riano: an acquittal may be reviewed by certiorari only for grave abuse amounting to lack of jurisdiction, such as a sham trial or denial of the prosecution's due process. The void acquittal does not place the accused in jeopardy.

S.title: Checkpoints, frisks, and consent
S.base: PO1 Cruz is assigned to a checkpoint along a national highway.

qs.q: Cruz shines a flashlight into a car and looks at the seats, without opening anything. Valid?
o: Yes. A routine checkpoint limited to a visual search is not unreasonable
No, any search needs a warrant
Only with the driver's written consent
Only after a prior tip
qs.ex: Valmonte v. De Villa (1990); People v. Vinecario (2004): checkpoints are not illegal per se. A visual inspection, with no search of the vehicle or body search of its occupants, is valid.

qs.tw: Cruz orders everyone out and opens the trunk and bags, for no reason other than that it is a checkpoint.
o: Yes, checkpoints allow full searches
No. An extensive checkpoint search needs probable cause
Yes, vehicles have no expectation of privacy
No, checkpoints are illegal per se
qs.ex: Valmonte v. De Villa: if a vehicle is extensively searched, it must be on probable cause that the motorist is an offender or the vehicle carries evidence of an offense.

qs.tw: Instead, Cruz had verified surveillance reports naming a specific van, its plate number, and the marijuana it would carry. He stops and searches it.
o: No, he needed a warrant
Yes; a moving vehicle may be searched without a warrant on probable cause
Yes, any vehicle may be searched at will
No, information can never be probable cause
qs.ex: Search of a moving vehicle (Carroll doctrine): warrantless search is allowed because the vehicle can quickly move, but only on probable cause, i.e., facts known to the officer reasonably showing it carries items subject to seizure (People v. Libnao).

qs.tw: Different stop: a jeepney driver signals to Cruz that a passenger is 'acting suspicious.' Cruz stops him and opens his bag, finding marijuana.
o: Yes, the driver's signal gave reasonable suspicion
No. The 'genuine reason' must come from the officer's own observation, not someone else's suspicion
Yes, because marijuana was found
Yes, because it happened at a checkpoint
qs.ex: People v. Cogaed (2014): the officer merely adopted the driver's suspicion. Compare Posadas and Manalili, where the officers themselves observed suspicious conduct.

qs.tw: The passenger said nothing and handed over the bag when told to open it.
o: Yes, he handed it over
No. Silence or passive conformity under coercive circumstances is not consent; the State must prove free and voluntary consent
Yes, consent may be implied from conduct
No, consent must always be written
qs.ex: People v. Cogaed; Veridiano v. People (2017): consent must be unequivocal, specific, intelligently given, and free from coercion, proven by clear and positive evidence.

qs.tw: The marijuana is excluded as fruit of the poisonous tree. It is the only evidence of the crime.
o: Acquittal; without the drugs, there is no corpus delicti
A new trial
Conviction on Cruz's testimony
Remand to the prosecutor
qs.ex: People v. Villareal (2013): where the excluded drug is the very corpus delicti, the accused must be acquitted.

qs.tw: Different case: police arrest Dan at his gate on a warrant, then search his whole house without a search warrant.
qs.q: Is the house search valid as incident to the arrest?
o: Yes, anything in the house may be searched
No. It covers only his person and the area within his immediate reach and control
Yes, if done within 24 hours
No, a search incident to arrest is never valid
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 13; People v. Lua (1996): the house was not within the arrestee's reach and control, so the search was not incident to the arrest.

S.title: Rights of the accused
S.base: Nestor is suspected of a robbery in which a guard was killed.

qs.q: Police place Nestor in a line-up, where a witness identifies him. He had no lawyer. Was his right to counsel violated?
o: Yes, counsel is required in every police procedure
No. A police line-up is not part of custodial investigation; the right to counsel does not yet attach
Yes, if he asked for a lawyer
No, because he was not yet charged in court
qs.ex: People v. Tolentino (2004): during a line-up, the accused is not yet being investigated, so the right to counsel cannot yet be claimed.

qs.tw: Next, police make Nestor re-enact the crime on video, without counsel.
o: Yes, it is physical evidence
No. A forced re-enactment falls under the right against self-incrimination
Yes, because it was recorded
Only against his co-accused
qs.ex: People v. Olvis (1987): forced re-enactments, like uncounselled and coerced confessions, are within the ban against self-incrimination.

qs.tw: Police also take a paraffin test on Nestor's hands over his objection.
o: Yes, he was compelled
No. The privilege covers only testimonial compulsion, not examination of the body
Yes, unless counsel was present
No, because paraffin tests are unreliable
qs.ex: The right against self-incrimination extends only to testimonial compulsion, not to examining the body of the accused.

qs.tw: At trial, the prosecution's eyewitness dies after direct examination, before cross, through no fault of Nestor.
qs.q: What happens to the direct testimony?
o: It stays in full
Nestor may have it stricken; testimony not subjected to cross-examination, through no fault of his, is generally stricken
It becomes a dying declaration
The trial starts over
qs.ex: Riano, citing People v. Seneris: one deprived of cross-examination without fault on his part is generally entitled to have the direct examination stricken.

qs.tw: Separately, the Ombudsman's preliminary investigation of a graft charge against Nestor, a barangay official, sat idle for six years with no explanation.
o: Speedy trial, but only once a case is in court
Speedy disposition of cases, which applies before any tribunal, including the Ombudsman during PI
None; PI is not part of the criminal action
Only an administrative complaint against the investigator
qs.ex: Tatad v. Sandiganbayan; Coscolluela v. Sandiganbayan; Cagang v. Sandiganbayan: speedy disposition applies to all proceedings, judicial or quasi-judicial. Inordinate, unexplained delay warrants dismissal.

qs.tw: At trial, the judge asks Nestor's alibi witnesses long, hostile questions, more than the prosecutor does.
o: Compulsory process
An impartial trial: the judge may ask clarificatory questions sparingly but must not act as an advocate
Confrontation
None; judges may question freely
qs.ex: Tabuena v. Sandiganbayan (1997): a judge who takes up the cudgels for the prosecution denies the "cold neutrality of an impartial judge." Mere sarcasm, without partiality, is not enough (People v. Moriera).

qs.tw: At the end, the evidence is evenly balanced: two credible accounts, one consistent with innocence.
o: Conviction, since the prosecution's account is credible
Acquittal, under the equipoise rule
A new trial
Judgment for the side with more witnesses
qs.ex: The equipoise rule follows from the presumption of innocence: when the evidence is evenly balanced, the accused is acquitted.

S.title: Bail: hearings and special cases
S.base: Victor is arrested and charged with child abuse under R.A. 7610, a bailable offense.

qs.q: The judge rules that Victor may post bail only after he is arraigned. Proper?
o: Yes, so he cannot avoid arraignment later
No. Bail cannot be conditioned on arraignment; he must stay free to move to quash before pleading
Yes, if the offense is serious
No, because posting bail waives arraignment
qs.ex: Lavides v. CA (2000): requiring arraignment first would force the accused to choose between a motion to quash (and delayed release) and giving it up.

qs.tw: The prosecutor proves that Victor is a flight risk.
o: Yes, flight risk justifies denial
No. When bail is a matter of right, flight risk only justifies a higher amount
Yes, if he has a passport
Only after conviction
qs.ex: San Miguel v. Maceda (2007): when bail is a matter of right, a high probability of flight gives the court no more discretion than to raise the bond, within the bar on excessive bail.

qs.tw: Change the charge: Victor is now charged with murder. After a hearing, the judge grants bail in a one-line order: "Bail granted."
o: Yes, the hearing is what counts
No. The order must summarize the prosecution's evidence and state the conclusion on whether evidence of guilt is strong
Yes, if the prosecutor did not object
No, murder is never bailable
qs.ex: Narciso v. Santa Romana-Cruz (2000): the judge decides on a summary of the evidence. A.M. No. 12-11-2-SC: the order, with a brief summary of the evidence and the conclusion, issues within 48 hours after the hearing.

qs.tw: Under the Guidelines, Victor's petition for bail (filed after the information) is heard.
qs.q: Within what period must it be resolved?
o: 10 days
30 days from the first hearing (20 days in drug cases)
90 days
Before the prosecution rests
qs.ex: A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: summary hearing after arraignment and pre-trial; resolved within a non-extendible 30 days from the first hearing, or 20 days in drug cases, without oral argument or memoranda.

qs.tw: The judge holds the hearing and denies bail.
qs.q: Besides reconsideration, what is Victor's remedy?
o: Appeal the denial to the CA
A petition for certiorari, if the denial was made with grave abuse of discretion
A motion to quash
None until judgment
qs.ex: People v. Gomez (2000): the remedy against an order denying bail is certiorari for grave abuse amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.

qs.tw: Different person: Hans faces extradition to the U.S. and asks for bail.
o: Bail is a matter of right, as in criminal cases
No right to bail; granted only on clear and convincing proof that he is not a flight risk or danger, plus special, humanitarian, and compelling circumstances
Discretionary, on preponderance of evidence
Bail is never available in extradition
qs.ex: Government of the U.S. v. Purganan (2002): extradition is not a criminal proceeding, so the constitutional right to bail does not apply; the exception requires the two-tier clear and convincing showing.

qs.tw: Different person: Lt. Reyes, a soldier facing court-martial, asks for bail.
o: Yes, the Constitution covers all persons
No. The right to bail has traditionally not been recognized in the military
Yes, if the offense is bailable under the RPC
Only with his commander's approval
qs.ex: Comendador v. Villa (1991): the unique structure of the military justifies exempting military personnel from the right to bail; the speedy trial right is emphasized instead.

S.title: Probable cause, review, and withdrawal
S.base: A complaint for estafa against Mila is filed with the city prosecutor. The penalty exceeds 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day.

qs.q: At a clarificatory hearing, Mila's lawyer insists on cross-examining the complainant. Allowed?
o: Yes, due process requires cross-examination
No. Parties may attend but have no right to cross-examine; they may submit questions to the investigating officer
Yes, if the prosecutor consents
Only if the complainant is a public officer
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 3(e): the parties may be present at the clarificatory hearing, but without the right to examine or cross-examine.

qs.tw: The prosecutor finds probable cause, and the DOJ Secretary affirms on review.
qs.q: How does Mila challenge the DOJ resolution in court?
o: Petition for review under Rule 43 with the CA
Petition for certiorari under Rule 65 with the CA, for grave abuse of discretion
Appeal to the RTC
Petition under Rule 45 to the SC
qs.ex: Riano: the DOJ Secretary's resolution is reviewable only for grave abuse of discretion, by Rule 65 certiorari filed with the CA. Rule 43 does not apply.

qs.tw: The information is filed in the RTC. Mila moves for a judicial determination of probable cause.
o: Hold a hearing on the motion
Deny it as a prohibited motion; the judge personally evaluates the prosecutor's resolution and evidence anyway
Return the case to the prosecutor
Issue a warrant automatically
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 5; A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: the motion is prohibited and superfluous, since the judge must personally evaluate the record with or without it.

qs.tw: The judge finds that the evidence clearly fails to show probable cause and dismisses the case.
o: Certiorari under Rule 65
Appeal; the dismissal is a final order
A motion to quash
None; jeopardy attached
qs.ex: Cajipe v. People (2014): a dismissal for lack of probable cause disposes of the case, so it is a final order; appeal, not certiorari, is the remedy.

qs.tw: Instead, the judge finds probable cause. After the information is filed, Mila moves for reinvestigation, arguing that the complainant's witnesses are not credible.
qs.q: How should the court treat it?
o: Grant it; reinvestigation is always allowed
Deny it as prohibited; credibility is an unmeritorious ground for reinvestigation
Grant it if filed within 15 days
Refer it to the DOJ
qs.ex: A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: a motion for reinvestigation on unmeritorious grounds, such as credibility, admissibility of evidence, innocence, or lack of due process when the accused was actually notified, is prohibited.

qs.tw: Later, the prosecutor moves to withdraw the information, and the court grants it.
qs.q: If the complainant wants to question the order, what is the remedy?
o: Certiorari, since the order is interlocutory
Appeal, since the order is final; it ends the case
A new complaint with the barangay
None; withdrawal is unreviewable
qs.ex: Riano, citing Santos v. Orda: an order granting the prosecution's motion to withdraw the information and dismissing the case is a final order, so appeal is the remedy.

qs.tw: Different case: Mila is the respondent in an Ombudsman graft complaint, and the Ombudsman finds probable cause.
qs.q: Where does she go to court?
o: Rule 43 petition to the CA
Rule 65 certiorari to the SC
Appeal to the Sandiganbayan
Rule 45 petition to the SC
qs.ex: Riano: in criminal cases, the Ombudsman's ruling goes to the SC by Rule 65, limited to grave abuse of discretion (Villanueva v. Ople).

S.title: Prescription, venue, and substitution
S.base: Arnel issues a bouncing check to Ben in Makati. Ben deposits it in Pasig, where it is dishonored.

qs.q: Where may the B.P. 22 case be filed?
o: Only in Makati, where the check was issued
In Makati or Pasig, where any element occurred; the first court to take cognizance excludes the other
Only where Ben lives
Only in Pasig, where it was dishonored
qs.ex: Riano: B.P. 22 is a transitory or continuing crime; the case may be filed where the check was drawn, issued, delivered, or dishonored (Rule 110, Sec. 15[a]).

qs.tw: B.P. 22 prescribes in 4 years. Ben filed his complaint with the Makati prosecutor 3 years and 11 months after the offense; the information reached court only after 4 years.
o: Yes, only filing in court interrupts prescription for special laws
No. Filing the complaint with the prosecutor for PI interrupted the period
Yes, B.P. 22 prescribes in 1 year
No, B.P. 22 does not prescribe
qs.ex: People v. Pangilinan (2012); Panaguiton v. DOJ (2008): for offenses under the RPC or special laws alike, filing the complaint with the prosecutor for PI interrupts prescription.

qs.tw: At trial, the public prosecutor is in the hospital. The judge lets the defense present two witnesses with no prosecutor present, then offers the prosecution a chance to cross them later.
o: Yes, the later cross cures it
No. Criminal cases are under the public prosecutor's direction and control; trial without him or an authorized private prosecutor is irregular and not cured by a later cross
Yes, if Ben was present
Yes, in B.P. 22 cases
qs.ex: Pinote v. Ayco (2005): letting the defense present evidence in the absence of a public prosecutor or a designated private prosecutor transgressed Rule 110, Sec. 5; a later chance to cross does not rectify it.

qs.tw: Different case: Ben is libeled in a newspaper printed and first published in Manila. Ben, a private person, lives in Cebu.
qs.q: Where may the libel case be filed?
o: Only in Manila
In Manila, where it was printed and first published, or in Cebu, where Ben resided
Anywhere the paper circulated
Only in Cebu
qs.ex: Art. 360 RPC, as amended: where the article was printed and first published, or where the offended party actually resided at the time (or held office, if a public officer).

qs.tw: Different case: Ben's wife suffers anguish in Manila because Ben carries on an affair in Singapore. She files a case for psychological violence under R.A. 9262.
qs.q: Can a Philippine court try it?
o: No, the affair happened abroad
Yes. The mental and emotional anguish, an element of the offense, is suffered here
Only if Ben returns
Only the Family Court of Singapore can
qs.ex: AAA v. BBB (2018): the Supreme Court upheld the trial court's jurisdiction; the offended wife was even allowed to appeal the dismissal directly in the interest of justice.

qs.tw: Different case: Arnel is charged with theft and pleads. The evidence shows he received the money lawfully as an agent and then misappropriated it.
qs.q: The prosecution wants to charge estafa instead. Amendment or substitution?
o: Amendment, without leave
Substitution, with leave: estafa is a different offense not included in theft; the theft case is dismissed once the new information is filed, with no double jeopardy
Amendment with leave, as a formal change
Neither; he must be acquitted
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 14 (second paragraph); Rule 119, Sec. 19; Teehankee v. Madayag: substitution presupposes a different offense, so the accused cannot claim double jeopardy. A new PI and a new plea are needed.

S.title: Plea bargaining and pre-trial, Guidelines era
S.base: Jojo, a detained accused, is charged in the RTC with illegal sale of shabu.

qs.q: Under the Guidelines, when must his arraignment and pre-trial be set?
o: Arraignment within 30 days of the court acquiring jurisdiction; pre-trial 30 days later
On the same date, within 10 days from the court's receipt of the case
Arraignment within 3 days; pre-trial within 10 days after
Pre-trial first, then arraignment
qs.ex: A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: arraignment and pre-trial are set on the same date, within 10 calendar days from receipt of the case for a detained accused, or 30 days from acquiring jurisdiction for one not detained.

qs.tw: Jojo offers to plead guilty to a lesser drug offense. The prosecutor objects only because Sec. 23 of R.A. 9165 bars plea bargaining in drug cases.
o: Yes, Sec. 23 bars plea bargaining in every drug case
No. Sec. 23 was struck down as unconstitutional; the plea is still subject to the required consent and the court's discretion
Yes, unless the drug is marijuana
No, plea bargaining is a right of the accused
qs.ex: Estipona v. Lobrigo (2017): Sec. 23 encroached on the Supreme Court's exclusive power to promulgate rules of procedure. A plea to a lesser offense remains discretionary, not a right.

qs.tw: Plea bargaining proceeds at arraignment.
qs.q: For a victimless crime like this, whose presence and consent does the Guidelines require?
o: The offended party's
The arresting officer's, with the public prosecutor's conformity
The DOJ Secretary's
No one's; the accused's offer is enough
qs.ex: A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: the private offended party in private crimes, or the arresting officer in victimless crimes, must be present to consent, with the conformity of the public prosecutor.

qs.tw: The plea to the lesser offense is accepted.
qs.q: What does the court do next?
o: Set the case for trial on the lesser offense
Render judgment immediately in the same proceedings
Refer the case to mediation
Require memoranda
qs.ex: A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: after plea bargaining, judgment shall be immediately rendered in the same proceedings.

qs.tw: Different case: Jojo is charged with robbery and wants to plead guilty to estafa.
o: Yes, estafa carries a lighter penalty
No. The lesser offense must be necessarily included in the offense charged; estafa is not included in robbery
Yes, with the offended party's consent
Yes, if made before trial
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 2; Daan v. Sandiganbayan: the elements of estafa are not included in robbery or theft.

qs.tw: Different case: a theft case in the MTC. At pre-trial, the accused and the complainant are absent though duly notified; defense counsel and the prosecutor are present.
o: No, the accused must be present
Yes; the court proceeds if they were duly notified and counsel and the prosecutor are present
No, the complainant must attend
Only if the accused waives in writing
qs.ex: A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: the court proceeds with pre-trial despite the absence of the accused or private complainant, if duly notified, so long as defense counsel and the public prosecutor are present.

qs.tw: Different case: a B.P. 22 case in the MTC. After arraignment and pre-trial, the parties are close to settling the civil liability.
o: The case is dismissed upon settlement
It is referred to mediation of the civil liability for a non-extendible 30 days; trial proceeds if mediation fails
It is suspended until payment
It is referred to barangay conciliation
qs.ex: A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: B.P. 22 is among the cases referred to the Philippine Mediation Center after arraignment and pre-trial, for 30 non-extendible days.

S.title: Civil liability beyond the basics
S.base: Rey, a bus driver for Star Lines, is convicted of reckless imprudence resulting in homicide and ordered to pay civil indemnity.
