qs.q: The writ of execution against Rey is returned unsatisfied; he is insolvent. Can the heirs go after Star Lines in the same criminal case?
o: No, Star Lines was not a party
Yes, on its subsidiary liability, after a hearing with notice proving it is the employer, is engaged in industry, Rey acted in the discharge of his duties, and Rey is insolvent
Yes, at once, without a hearing
Only in a separate quasi-delict case
qs.ex: Arts. 102–103 RPC; Galang v. People (2010): the subsidiary liability is deemed written into the judgment and is enforced in the same criminal case, in a hearing set for that purpose with due notice to the employer.

qs.tw: Instead, before the criminal case, the heirs had sued Star Lines for quasi-delict. Rey argues that the civil case is a prejudicial question to his criminal case.
o: Yes, the issue of negligence is the same
No. An independent civil action does not operate as a prejudicial question
Yes, because it was filed first
Only if the heirs agree
qs.ex: Riano: independent civil actions (Arts. 32, 33, 34, 2176) proceed independently of the criminal case and do not operate as prejudicial questions.

qs.tw: Different case: Rey is the accused in an estafa case and, before any civil case is filed, petitions to suspend the criminal case for a prejudicial question.
qs.q: How is the petition treated under the Guidelines?
o: As a meritorious motion, set for hearing
As a prohibited motion, because no civil case has yet been filed
As a motion to quash
As a request for reinvestigation
qs.ex: A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: a petition to suspend the criminal action on a prejudicial question is prohibited when no civil case has been filed. If the civil case was filed first, it is meritorious.

qs.tw: Different case: a public employee is acquitted of malversation on reasonable doubt. An administrative case for the same act is pending.
qs.q: Does the acquittal end the administrative case?
o: Yes, the facts are the same
No; the administrative case needs only substantial evidence
Yes, if the acquittal is final
No, but it must be suspended until the civil aspect ends
qs.ex: Gupilan-Aguilar v. Ombudsman (2014): acquittal does not conclude the administrative case, which requires only substantial evidence.

qs.tw: Different case: Odin is charged with rape. A child is born of the crime. The civil action has not been waived, reserved, or filed separately.
qs.q: May the court order support pendente lite in the criminal case?
o: No, provisional remedies are limited to attachment
Yes; civil provisional remedies, including support pendente lite, are available in connection with the civil action deemed instituted
Only after conviction
No, support needs a separate family case
qs.ex: Rule 127, Sec. 1; Riano: provisional remedies apply as far as applicable to the civil action deemed instituted, including support pendente lite (Rule 61, Sec. 6).

qs.tw: Different case: the complainant had Odin's property attached in the criminal case. Odin is later acquitted, and the attachment caused him losses.
qs.q: When does Odin prove those damages?
o: Only in a separate civil suit
When he presents his evidence at trial; the accused may prove damages from a provisional remedy issued in the case
On appeal only
He cannot; attachments carry no liability
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 11(b): the accused may present evidence to prove his defense and damages, if any, arising from the issuance of a provisional remedy in the case.

S.title: Judgment: form, mode, and offer
S.base: Edgar is tried in the RTC for rape.

qs.q: The judge who heard all the witnesses retires. Her successor writes the decision from the records. Edgar says the decision is void. Is it?
o: Yes, only the judge who saw the witnesses may decide
No. A judge who did not hear the witnesses may decide on the records
Yes, unless Edgar consents
No, but the witnesses must be recalled first
qs.ex: People v. Alfredo (2010): relying on the records, rather than observing the witnesses' demeanor, does not by itself make the judgment erroneous, especially where the record supports it.

qs.tw: The information charged rape by sexual intercourse. At trial, only rape by sexual assault (insertion of an object) is proved.
qs.q: Can Edgar be convicted of rape by sexual assault?
o: Yes, rape is rape
No. The two modes differ substantially; he may be convicted at most of acts of lasciviousness
Yes, if he did not object
No, he must be acquitted outright
qs.ex: People v. Caoili (2017): rape by sexual intercourse and rape by sexual assault are substantially distinct; conviction for the unalleged mode violates the right to be informed. The lesser offense of acts of lasciviousness may be found.

qs.tw: Different variance: the information alleged "force and intimidation," but the victim testified she was asleep. Edgar did not object to the evidence.
o: Yes, the information must match the proof exactly
No. A variance in the manner of commission binds the accused if he fails to object
Yes, unless the information is amended
No, because sleep is a form of force
qs.ex: People v. Abella (2009): a variance in the mode of commission is binding on the accused if he does not object to evidence showing a different manner.

qs.tw: To prove qualified rape, the prosecution marked the victim's birth certificate at pre-trial but never formally offered it.
qs.q: Can the court use it to prove minority?
o: Yes, it was marked
No. Evidence not formally offered cannot be considered; the conviction is for simple rape
Yes, the accused did not object
Yes, birth certificates are public documents
qs.ex: People v. Villanueva (2010): the court shall consider no evidence not formally offered (Rule 132, Sec. 34). Qualified rape was reduced to simple rape.

qs.tw: Under the Guidelines, the case is submitted for decision.
qs.q: By when must the decision be promulgated?
o: Within 30 days
Within 90 days from submission, on a date announced in open court
Within 3 months, as the Constitution allows
Whenever the transcripts are complete
qs.ex: A.M. No. 15-06-10-SC: the promulgation date is announced in open court and set not more than 90 calendar days from submission. Missing transcripts do not justify delay.

qs.tw: Edgar is acquitted. The judgment only says the prosecution "failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt."
o: Nothing more
Whether the act or omission from which civil liability might arise did not exist
The penalty that would have applied
The participation of each witness
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 2: an acquittal must state whether the evidence absolutely failed or merely failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and in either case determine whether the act giving rise to civil liability did not exist.
